title: Act I, Scene III

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Neither a borrower nor a lender be” slowly and put it in my own words: Sending Laertes off to France, Polonius gives a list of maxims, including not to borrow or lend money. Next, craft. I notice the balanced, proverb-like phrase "neither... nor," typical of his tidy, quotable advice. The strongest word is “borrower”: it frames life in terms of money and reputation, his main concerns. Then, effect. What does Polonius's advice show about his values? My answer: Polonius cares most about appearances and prudence; his advice sounds wise but is calculating, and his later spying shows the same concern with managing how things look.
